tags.meaning: A haal is a word or sentence that describes the condition of someone or something at the moment the main action happens.
The zul haal is the person or thing whose condition the haal is describing.
A haal that is just one word, not a full sentence, for example an active participle or a verbal noun.
A haal made of a whole sentence that starts with a noun and simply states a fact.
A haal made of a whole sentence that starts with a verb and simply states a fact.

tags.en: Command Sentence, Not Allowed as Haal
tags.meaning: A sentence that commands, forbids, or asks a question can never be used as a haal.
This is the letter waw placed at the start of a sentence to mark it as describing a state.
The haal waw must be used, most often before a noun-sentence haal that has no pronoun linking it back to the zul haal.
The haal waw is allowed but not required, so the sentence is correct with or without it.
The haal waw cannot be used at all, for example before a present-tense verb haal that has no qad in front of it.
A pronoun that ties a sentence or phrase back to the noun it is about, as in a haal sentence or a نعت سببي.
When a past-tense verb is the haal, it usually needs qad before it, to bring its meaning close to the present moment.
When a present-tense verb is the haal, whether the haal waw is allowed depends on the word, such as la, ma, lamma, or qad, that comes right before it.
A haal that describes a state which has not happened yet at the moment of the main action, so it points forward in time.
A noun that is not built from a verb can only work as a haal if it can be understood to carry an action-like meaning.
A noun in the accusative case that gives the reason why the main action was done.
A true mafool lahu must itself be a plain verbal noun, happen at the same time as, and be done by the same doer as, the main action.
When a mafool lahu is missing one of its required conditions, the word for (a lam) is understood before it instead.
A noun that tells when or where the main action happened.
A mafool feehi that names a time, like today or at night.
A mafool feehi that names a place, like in front of or above.
A small set of unrestricted place and time words, such as before and after, that take a fixed dhamma ending when the noun they would normally attach to is left out.
A tanween that stands in for something dropped, whether a single letter, a whole word, or a whole sentence.
A tanween that shows a noun is unspecified rather than a particular one.
The regular tanween on a fully declinable noun, showing it behaves like a firmly established, normal noun.
A noun in the accusative case naming something that was present together with another noun while the action happened.
The waw right before the mafool ma'ahu, meaning along with rather than and.
Joining two equal nouns together with a waw meaning and, so both are treated as doing the same action.
A pronoun stuck onto the end of a preposition or noun, such as the -hi in bihi.
A pronoun stuck onto a verb showing who did the action, such as the -tu in fatahtu.
A word, such as an active participle, that behaves like a verb even though it is not one.
A verb whose meaning only makes sense with two or more people doing it together, like arguing with each other, so the second noun must be atf and can never be mafool ma'ahu.
The noun joined by atf to the noun before it, standing as its equal partner rather than a mere companion.
A question that asks what a grammar term means or what category it falls into.
A question that asks you to choose between two similar-looking options, such as atf versus ma'iyyah, or which of the five maf'ool types a word is.
A question that gives a sentence with an error in it and asks how many mistakes there are and how to fix them.
A question that gives an English sentence and asks which of two Arabic versions correctly expresses the grammar point.
A question that gives a real sentence and asks you to apply the grammar rules to it.
A verbal noun from the same root as the verb, placed after it to stress that the action happened, or to say what kind it was, or how many times.
The noun in the accusative case that the action is done to.
A word that is not the verbal noun itself but stands in its place and still carries the sense of how the action happened.
Maa and laa can act like the word laysa (is not): the subject stays in its normal form and the predicate is put into the accusative case, unless something in the sentence cancels this.
A laa that denies an entire kind of thing all at once, such as no book at all rather than just one book, and gives its noun a special fixed or accusative ending.
A word made of laa plus taa that is only used with words for time, and always leaves one of its two parts, the subject or the predicate, unsaid.
The letter in used to mean not; some grammarians say it works like maa and puts the predicate in the accusative case, though most say it has no effect on the sentence's case endings.
A phrase that describes something connected to the noun before it, rather than describing that noun directly.
The noun that an adjective phrase (نعت) is describing.
The word or phrase that gets excluded from what was just said, usually right after إلا.
A word such as إلا, غير, سوى, عدا, خلا or حاشا that introduces an exception in a sentence.
The larger group or statement that something is being excepted out of.
The classification questions used for an exception sentence: is it positive or negative, is the excepted-from group missing or present, and is the exception connected to or separate from that group.
A word like إلا that, instead of making an exception, is used to mean only, limiting the sentence to just one thing.
A noun that takes tanween and shows all three case endings in the normal way.
A noun that cannot take tanween and, when majroor, takes a fatha instead of a kasra, because one strong cause or two causes together are present.
Being a proper name. It blocks tanween only together with a second cause, such as femininity, foreignness or a verb pattern.
Being a describing word. It blocks tanween together with a second cause, such as a verb pattern or an added alif and nun.
A feminine name, with or without a taa marbuta; together with being a proper name it blocks tanween.
A proper name taken from a language other than Arabic, such as إبراهيم; together with being a name it blocks tanween.
A word turned from its original pattern, such as عمر from عامر or ثلاث from ثلاثة ثلاثة.
A noun on a pattern that belongs to verbs, such as أحمد or أكبر.
An alif and nun added at the end of the word, as in عثمان or غضبان.
A feminine alif at the end, short (ى) as in حبلى or stretched (اء) as in حمراء; this cause alone is enough to block tanween.
A broken plural on the furthest plural pattern, such as مساجد or مصابيح; this cause alone is enough to block tanween.
